title: Georgia and Armenia: The Caucasus Road Trip
metaDescription: A two-week Georgia and Armenia itinerary — Tbilisi, the Greater Caucasus, wine country, Yerevan and the monasteries — with costs, driving and border advice.
excerpt: Mountains, 8,000-year-old wine, cliff-edge monasteries and some of the most generous hospitality in the world, at prices that barely register.
author: Trypinn Team
content:
The Caucasus is the kind of region that people return from evangelising about. Mountains that rival the Alps with none of the infrastructure or prices. Churches carved into cliffs. A wine tradition that predates the European one by several thousand years. And a culture of hospitality so insistent that declining food is genuinely difficult.

Georgia and Armenia pair naturally — a land border, a short drive between the capitals, and two very different countries despite the shared neighbourhood.

## When to Go

- **May to June** — green, wildflowers, comfortable. The best window
- **September to October** — harvest season in Georgian wine country, clear mountain weather, still warm
- **July and August** — hot in the lowlands, ideal in the mountains. Busiest
- **Winter** — Tbilisi and Yerevan are atmospheric and cheap; many mountain roads close, including the road to Ushguli

## Georgia

**Tbilisi — 3 days**

One of the most characterful capitals in the region. Sulphur baths in the old town under brick domes, wooden balconies on crumbling facades, Soviet modernism, a cable car to the fortress, and a restaurant and bar scene that has become genuinely excellent.

Walk the **Old Town** and **Abanotubani**, take the cable car to **Narikala**, visit the **Dry Bridge Market**, and eat. Tbilisi is a food city.

**Kazbegi and the Military Highway — 2 days**

The drive north from Tbilisi to **Stepantsminda** is the country's signature road trip, climbing through the Greater Caucasus. The destination is **Gergeti Trinity Church**, a lone 14th-century church on a ridge beneath the 5,000-metre Mount Kazbek. It is, genuinely, one of the great views in Europe.

You can drive up or walk it in about an hour and a half. Walk it.

**Kakheti wine country — 2 days**

Georgia has been making wine for around 8,000 years, in buried clay **qvevri**, and the tradition is unbroken. Kakheti is the heartland: **Sighnaghi**, a walled hilltop town overlooking the Alazani valley; **Telavi**; and dozens of family wineries where a tasting means sitting down with a family.

Georgian wine is a genuinely distinct category — amber wines fermented on the skins in clay, unlike anything in Western Europe.

![Georgia travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1561731172-9d906d7b13bf?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

**Svaneti — 3 days**

The most remote and most spectacular region. **Mestia** is the hub; **Ushguli**, one of Europe's highest permanently inhabited settlements, sits beneath Mount Shkhara surrounded by medieval defensive tower houses.

The road is long and rough, and the four-day **Mestia to Ushguli trek** is one of the best walks in the Caucasus, staying in guesthouses each night. Accessible roughly June to October.

**Other options:** the **Black Sea** at Batumi, with its unusual skyline; **Vardzia**, a cave monastery city carved into a cliff; **Borjomi** and its mineral springs; and **Tusheti**, even more remote than Svaneti and reached by one of the world's more alarming mountain roads.

## Armenia

Cross at the **Sadakhlo–Bagratashen** border, or take the direct Tbilisi–Yerevan road, roughly six hours.

**Yerevan — 2 days**

A pink tuff-stone city built around a grand Soviet plan, with Mount Ararat — in Turkey, but visually dominant and emotionally central to Armenia — on the horizon on clear days.

- **The Cascade** — a monumental stairway with sculpture, and the view from the top
- **Republic Square** and the singing fountains
- **The Armenian Genocide Memorial**, essential context for understanding the country
- **Matenadaran**, the manuscript institute
- **GUM Market** for food, and a café culture that runs late

![Georgia travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1583610261946-5d88e555be93?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

**The monasteries**

Armenia was the first state to adopt Christianity, and its monasteries are the country's defining sight — almost all of them in spectacular natural settings.

- **Geghard** — partly carved directly into rock, with extraordinary acoustics. Nearby **Garni** is a Hellenistic temple
- **Khor Virap** — a monastery on a small hill directly beneath Ararat. The most photographed view in Armenia
- **Tatev** — reached by the world's longest reversible cable car over a gorge, on a promontory above a canyon. The best single day in the country
- **Noravank** — at the end of a red rock canyon
- **Haghpat and Sanahin** — UNESCO-listed, in the north near the Georgian border, easy to combine with the crossing

**Lake Sevan** — a vast high-altitude lake with a peninsula monastery, good for a stop between Yerevan and the north.

**Dilijan** — forested, cooler, sometimes called Armenia's Switzerland, with good walking.

## Practicalities

- **Visas** — Georgia allows visa-free entry for an unusually long list of nationalities, often for a full year. Armenia is visa-free or e-visa for most. Both are outside Schengen, so days do not count against your European allowance
- **Driving** — the best way to see both. Roads range from good highway to rough mountain track. Svaneti and Tusheti need a 4WD. Driving standards are assertive; be defensive. Check whether your rental permits crossing the border — many do not, and the common solution is to rent separately in each country
- **Border** — the Georgia–Armenia crossing is straightforward. Note that **Armenia's borders with Turkey and Azerbaijan are closed**, and that travelling to Azerbaijan after visiting certain areas can create complications. Plan the regional routing carefully
- **Money** — Georgian lari and Armenian dram. ATMs are widely available in cities, cash needed in villages
- **Language** — Georgian and Armenian, each with its own script. Russian is widely understood; English is growing among younger people
- **Costs** — outstanding value. Budget $30–45 a day, mid-range $65–100, comfortable $140–230

## The Food

A genuine reason to go.

**Georgian:** khachapuri (cheese bread, with an Adjarian version containing egg and butter), khinkali (soup dumplings, eaten by hand, do not eat the top knot), badrijani nigvzit (aubergine with walnut paste), lobio, and an enormous range of walnut and herb dishes. Vegetarians eat extremely well.

**Armenian:** lavash bread baked in a clay oven, khorovats (barbecue), dolma, apricots and pomegranates, and excellent brandy.

The **supra** — a Georgian feast with a tamada leading formal toasts — is a cultural institution, and being invited to one is the trip's highlight for most people.

## A Two-Week Route

- **Days 1–3** — Tbilisi
- **Days 4–5** — Kazbegi and the Military Highway
- **Days 6–7** — Kakheti wine country
- **Days 8–10** — Svaneti, or Vardzia and Borjomi if the mountain roads are closed
- **Day 11** — cross to Armenia via Haghpat and Sanahin
- **Days 12–13** — Yerevan, Khor Virap, Garni and Geghard
- **Day 14** — Tatev and the Vorotan gorge

With three weeks, add Tusheti in Georgia and Dilijan and Lake Sevan in Armenia.

Two countries, two rental cars, a border crossing and a lot of mountain driving means this trip lives or dies on the route. Getting it laid out properly before booking anything — which country you start in, where each car goes back, which mountain roads are open in your month — is the whole planning job. Doing it in a shared plan on **Trypinn** makes the driving days visible, which is exactly where this itinerary tends to go wrong.
